messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 30-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a curriculum designer for a mid-sized educational nonprofit in Atlanta. He presents as soft-spoken and carefully composed, though the effort that composure requires becomes apparent over the course of the first few sessions. He sought help after a colleague noticed him standing frozen in the office kitchen, unable to move, following a moment he could not easily explain.

The relationship had lasted fourteen months. His former partner's abuse was not constant — it arrived in cycles, punctuated by periods of warmth that Kofi now understands were part of the pattern, though understanding this has done little to diminish the damage. The worst incident occurred on a Saturday evening when his partner had been drinking heavily. Kofi remembers the smell of alcohol on his breath before the first blow, and the acrid, burning smell that drifted in from something left too long on the stove — a detail that lodged itself in his nervous system with a precision his conscious mind could not have managed. He was struck repeatedly, mostly to the face and torso. He remembers lying on the floor, certain he was going to be seriously hurt, the terror absolute and unambiguous. His partner said nothing was going to happen to him and laughed. Kofi did not call the police. He left the apartment the next morning and never returned. Nothing formal was ever done.

In the months that followed, his body did not allow him to simply move on. When the memories return — and they return without warning — Kofi does not experience them as recollections. He feels them. A dull, pressured ache spreads across his ribs and jaw, the same places that absorbed the blows, and the terror he felt on that floor reconstitutes itself with an immediacy that leaves him gripping the edge of whatever surface is nearest. These memories carry their own sensory world: he can sometimes smell both the alcohol and the faint burn, even in a clean, quiet room. And it is precisely this quality of the memories — their physicality, their insistence on the present tense — that makes certain moments in his daily life so treacherous. The smell of alcohol at a work social event, or the burnt odour from a toaster in the office break room, does not remind Kofi of what happened. It returns him there, pulling the full memory forward with a force that bypasses any intention he has to stay grounded in the present. Even a colleague's offhand comment about family — the kind of remark that would pass unnoticed in any other context — can be enough, because his partner had frequently invoked Kofi's family during episodes, weaponising them, and those associations are now embedded in the architecture of his fear.

What makes this harder still is what these intrusions confirm to him about himself. Each time a trigger pulls the memory forward, and each time the memory surfaces on its own, Kofi is left with a set of convictions that have grown more entrenched over time. He had come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that the person he was before — curious, socially at ease, someone who trusted his own judgment — no longer exists. What replaced him is someone he does not recognise and does not particularly like. He is also haunted by a sense of injustice that has no outlet: what was done to him was real, it was serious, and it was never acknowledged by anyone with the authority to name it as wrong. Beneath both of these runs something more visceral — a feeling of contamination, as though the abuse left something on him that ordinary living cannot wash off. These appraisals are not beliefs he holds abstractly; they are conclusions the memories keep re-teaching him, and the triggers keep re-confirming.

At work, Kofi has quietly reorganised his days to avoid the kitchen between ten and noon, when colleagues tend to gather there with coffee and conversation. He has declined three team lunches. His manager has noticed he seems withdrawn, and a project review was recently delayed because Kofi had not been able to concentrate long enough to finish the accompanying documentation.

What finally brought him in was not the incident in the kitchen, exactly, but what he thought afterward: that he had no idea how to get himself back, or whether there was anything left to return to. What he is most afraid of is that the contamination is permanent. What he is most hoping for — though he struggles to say it directly — is that someone will tell him it is not.
